newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Rebels abduct 12 town councilors in north Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Rebels abduct 12 town councilors in north Colombia.

text.p: Leftist rebels kidnapped at least 12 town councilors in two communities in northern Colombia as part of their campaign to sabotage local elections in October, authorities said on Sunday.

In Simiti, in the northern province of Bolivar, the entire town council -- nine officials, including the town treasurer -- was seized on the way to a meeting on Saturday, police sources said. The seizure was carried out on the orders of one of the guerrilla armies that operate in the area, the sources said.

And in San Pablo, also in Bolivar, three councilors were kdinapped in similar circumstances. Provincial governor Miguel Navas blamed both abductions on the Cuban-inspired National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second-largest guerrilla force, set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966.
"We were not able to get official confirmation of these incidents until Sunday morning," Navas told reporters. "Nine council members were taken from Simiti and at least three more from San Pablo."

An NTC television news program showed the ELN's trademark black-and-red flag flying over some villages in Simiti, a town of about 8,000 inhabitants. Simiti has had no police presence since about 100 rebels overran the town on June 30, destroying the barracks and killing three policemen.
No demands have yet been made for concessions that would gain the officials' release, the spokesman said.
Earlier this month, the ELN kidnapped five mayors in the southern province of Narino and killed a senator in the northeastern province of Norte de Santander.

The larger rebel army of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), meanwhile, has forced candidates for the Oct. 26 mayoral elections to withdraw in some towns in southern and eastern Colombia.

Both guerrilla groups and right-wing paramilitary forces have pledged to disrupt the elections, in which provincial governors will also be elected, and have threatened to kill any candidates of opposing political views who dare to campaign in their zones of influence.
Gilberto Toro, head of the Colombian Association of Municipalities, said the rising violence meant it would be impossible to guarantee free and fair elections.
"From these actions, it is clear the paramilitaries and the guerrillas have control of large parts of the country. There are not sufficient guarantees for the October elections," he said.

But both he and Interior Minister Carlos Holmes stopped short of suggesting the coming vote should be suspended. In comments to reporters, Holmes said he would be evaluating the situation in each of Colombia's approximately 1,100 municipalities before proposing measures to guarantee the safety of voters and candidates.

In a separate incident in the northern province of Cesar, the badly charred bodies of four men were found dumped outside the provincial capital, Valledupar, police said. The motives for the killings were not immediately clear.
